questions.stem: A student investigates the reaction of aqueous sodium hydroxide with two different aqueous solutions of hydrochloric acid, solution X and solution Y. She carries out two experiments. Experiment 1 Using a measuring cylinder, she pours 20 $ cm^{3} $ of aqueous sodium hydroxide into a conical flask and records its temperature. Using a burette, she adds 5 $ cm^{3} $ of solution X to the conical flask. She stirs the mixture with the thermometer and records the temperature. She adds further 5 $ cm^{3} $ volumes of solution X and stirs with the thermometer. She records the temperature after each addition of solution X. She stops when a total of $ 4 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of solution X has been added. She empties the burette and rinses it first with water and then with solution Y. She then fills the burette with solution Y. She repeats the experiment using solution Y. The table shows the results she obtains in Experiment 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plot the results for Experiment 1 on the grid. Draw a straight line of best fit through the first three points and a second straight line of best fit through the last six points. Make sure that the two straight lines cross. Volume of solution X added in $ cm^{3} $

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the graph to determine the volume of solution X that will produce the maximum temperature rise when added to $ 2 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of the aqueous sodium hydroxide. volume of solution X = ... $ \mathrm{c m}^{3} $

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Use the graph to determine the maximum temperature rise. maximum temperature rise = $ \mathrm{^{\circ} C} $

parts.label: c
parts.text: Why did the student rinse the burette first with water, and then with solution Y, before performing Experiment 2? solution Y

parts.label: d
parts.text: The maximum temperature rise in Experiment 2 was less than that in Experiment 1. Suggest a reason why.

questions.stem: Potassium hydrogencarbonate （ $ \mathrm{KHCO}_{3} $ ）decomposes on heating. Three possible equations for the decomposition are $\mathrm {e q u a t i o n 1} \quad 2 \mathrm {K H C O} _ {3} (\mathrm {s}) \rightarrow \mathrm {K} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {s}) + 2 \mathrm {C O} _ {2} (\mathrm {g}) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {g})$ equation 2 $ \mathrm{K H C O}_{3} ( \mathrm{s} ) \rightarrow \mathrm{K O H} ( \mathrm{s} )+\mathrm{C O}_{2} ( \mathrm{g} ) $ $\mathrm {e q u a t i o n 3} \quad 2 \mathrm {K H C O} _ {3} (\mathrm {s}) \rightarrow \mathrm {K} _ {2} \mathrm {C O} _ {3} (\mathrm {s}) + \mathrm {C O} _ {2} (\mathrm {g}) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {g})$ When 8.00 g of potassium hydrogencarbonate is heated until it is fully decomposed, 5.52 g of solid is formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the table by calculating the amount, in moles, of each solid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the information in the table to explain which equation, 1, 2 or 3, represents the decomposition of potassium hydrogencarbonate.
